channel.title: Canopticon
channel.description: Questions researched in depth, and articles written from what the research found.

item.title: Portraiture as a research method: Sara Lawrence-Lightfoot's "painting with words", how it differs from ethnography, and the case against it
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Portraiture puts the researcher's own judgement at the centre of a study and measures success by whether readers recognise the truth of the portrait, not by whether anyone could repeat it. Its sharpest critic says that leaves no way to check the portraitist; its founder's answer is that a visible self demands more discipline, not less.

item.title: How investigative YouTube video essays are built: the cold open, the late turn to meaning, and the channels that borrow the form without the evidence
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: The strongest forensic video essays open on an artifact, walk through evidence in the order a viewer would experience it, and say what it all means only late in the video. That delayed turn is what persuades, which is why the same structure works just as well for channels whose evidence does not hold up.

item.title: Paying to reach curious readers in 2026: ChatGPT ads, feed ads, paid newsletter recommendations, and the labelling rules
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: ChatGPT now sells self-serve ads, but they cost about 3–8× more per impression than feed ads and are hard to measure, so the cheapest curious readers are still on Meta and Reddit. An ad can be the whole useful answer and still carry its label: the rules draw the line at fake people and hidden sponsors, not at ads that are worth reading.

item.title: How Canada's public-sector employees vote: the Canadian Election Study evidence, Ottawa's ridings, and the union endorsements
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Public-sector workers in Canada lean modestly left of private-sector workers, and most of that lean belongs to unionized professionals and managers. The city crews whose unions endorse the NDP vote much like their private-sector counterparts, and no released poll gives a party-by-party split to settle it.

item.title: Paying yourself to do your own tasks: what the incentive trials show, and whether an earn-back subscription could work
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Financial incentives move behaviour while they run, and losses move people more than equal gains. Paying yourself a wage from your own pocket removes most of what the trials rely on; a subscription you earn back by doing the work is a loss-framed stake, and the research rates it the version most likely to work. Nobody has tested it.

item.title: Canadian recessions and the mortgage channel: rate decisions, CMHC, and five decades of housing-led downturns
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Every major Canadian downturn since 1980 carries a monetary-policy fingerprint, and housing is how the decision reaches people. The clearest case is 1990, where the campaign overshot its own target and Toronto prices did not pass their 1989 peak until 2002.

item.title: Temporary foreign workers and Canadian innovation: what the automation evidence shows, and the study nobody has run
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: The research that says immigration drives innovation studies points-selected skilled migration. Canada's intake since 2016 has been mostly temporary and low-wage, and the causal work on cheap labour runs the other way — a 1% rise in low-skill wages lifts automation patenting 2–5%. The Canadian version of that study has never been done.

item.title: Whey protein in hot black coffee: why it curdles, what the heat-stable versions cost, and what is coming
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Collagen disappears into a hot cup; whey turns it into pale lumps that smell of sulfur. Coffee's acidity sits almost exactly where whey is least stable, and it is served above the temperature that unfolds the protein. The heat-stable ingredients that exist solve it by cutting the protein up, which makes it bitter.

item.title: Bill C-11 and Canadian creators in 2026: what the CRTC has actually imposed, and what is still a prediction
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Creators were told the Online Streaming Act would cost them their foreign audiences by teaching recommendation systems that Canadian videos go unwatched. Three years after royal assent the regulator has imposed no discoverability requirement on anyone, the money is stayed by a court, and no study has measured the harm.

item.title: Topping up low wages in Canada: the Canada Workers Benefit, employer capture, and the workers who never file
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Canada already runs the alternative to a basic income — a refundable credit that tops up low earnings automatically. Two things decide whether it works: employers absorb part of any wage subsidy where no floor exists, and about 9% of eligible earners never file a return.

item.title: How YouTube, Instagram and TikTok rank video in 2026: satisfaction signals, AI content understanding, and penalties for reposting
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Recommendation feeds have stopped scoring behaviour alone. A language model now watches the content and judges it — better than the crowd-sourced raters it replaced — while reposting is penalised in the ranking itself. Much of what creators are taught describes the system of a decade ago.

item.title: Measuring the economy with new instruments: scraped prices, card-spending trackers and satellite imagery
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Four old arguments explain why an economy resists being computed, and none of them have gone away. What computation did change is measurement — scraped prices, card records and satellite images that report what is happening weeks before the official numbers do.

item.title: Immigrants, temporary residents and Canada's job growth since 2020: what the Labour Force Survey can and cannot show
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Nearly all of Canada's post-pandemic job growth went to immigrants and temporary residents. But no Canadian government table publishes that split the way the American one does — every version of the figure is built by hand from an annual series that undercounts the very group it counts.

item.title: Missed workouts and broken streaks: how fast strength, mood and habit actually decay
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Two weeks away from the gym costs almost nothing in muscle — strength holds and the body keeps a record that makes the regain fast. What drains in that time is mood, dopamine tone and the automatic habit, which is exactly what restarting runs on.

item.title: Alcohol blackouts: how ethanol blocks memory formation, and why drinking speed decides it
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: In an alcohol blackout the drinker is awake, talking and deciding, while the brain's ability to save the night is chemically held shut. Nothing comes back afterwards because nothing was stored — and how fast the drinking goes decides whether it happens at all.

item.title: Fred Hutch's HSV gene therapy in 2026: mouse and guinea-pig results, no human trial, and the antivirals arriving first
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: A gene therapy clears up to 97% of dormant herpes in mice. In the animal that relapses the way people do it clears above 30%, nobody has filed to test it in a person, and the drugs arriving first suppress the virus rather than remove it.

item.title: Job guarantees in Austria, France and India: employment effects, cost per job, and the designs that trap people
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: A job for anyone who wants one sounds utopian. It has been tried — in an Austrian town, in 83 French territories and across rural India. It works, it costs money, and the design decides whether it is a springboard or a trap.

item.title: Language models and idea diversity: homogenisation within a session, across users, and between companies
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Ask a language model for something new and it pulls toward what everyone else would say — across companies, over long sessions, and across everyone using it. Real novelty has a shape the models do not reach for on their own.

item.title: Opioid deaths and overdose calls in Hamilton: why the two counts moved in opposite directions
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Hamilton's opioid deaths have fallen every year since 2021, while paramedic calls for overdoses more than doubled. The death count is measuring a drug supply that no longer exists.

item.title: Canada's short-term rental rules: supply, prices, and the mid-term rental tier that never formed
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Short-term rentals add flexible supply, and competition lowers prices. Canadian cities banned them anyway — and cut off a tier between a hotel and a lease just as it was forming.

item.title: Canada's short-term rental bans and rents: what returned to the long-term market, and what actually moved prices
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Canadian cities restricted short-term rentals to bring homes back to renters. Few came back, rents fell for other reasons, and the bans squeezed a new kind of housing that sits between a hotel and a lease.

item.title: Why people keep scrolling: habit, infinite feeds, and the evidence against the dopamine explanation
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: The best evidence says people keep scrolling because of habit and a feed that never ends — not because of a dopamine jackpot. And engagement-ranked feeds keep showing people what they say they do not want.

item.title: Unverified hunches in AI-assisted software work: the certainty handoff and one-sided memory
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: A hunch that feels right gets handed to a collaborator as if it had been checked. When the collaborator is an AI that starts every session blank, nobody checks it at all.

item.title: Krasis
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: The synthesis of the series. McLuhan said every medium changes the ratio among our senses; the paper series tests that literally, from ADHD and typing to drugs and addiction, and find one configuration that media, drugs and illness all re-temper.

item.title: Exocrasis
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: The computing environment, not the screen, is the medium: keyboard, memory, search and network move part of the configuration of the senses and of memory outside the body.

item.title: Heterocrasis
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: ADHD as a different starting balance of the senses. The strongest difference is in overall gain; the body and inner speech are mixed; binding is not looser.

item.title: Pharmakrasis
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Each class of drug sets its own balance of the senses — and the evidence for that is better than for any medium. When a drug meets a medium, as music does in psychedelic therapy, the two make a third thing.

item.title: Narcocrasis
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: In dependence, what goes unseen is not the drug but the shifted baseline: the allostatic state is the medium, the drug its content. Two routes back — one turns the gain down, one makes the ground visible.

item.title: Fixed times versus flexible routines in exercise habits: what the paid-to-exercise trials found
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Paid to exercise at a set time, people did less than those paid to exercise whenever they liked — and quit faster afterwards. What helps is a fixed start and an open workout.

item.title: Typomora
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: McLuhan said electric media would bring back the voice. For fifty years computers made us type instead. The delay was the keyboard, not a mistake in the theory — and it is ending.

item.title: Sensory syncrasis
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: McLuhan meant his "sense ratios" literally. The brain science he reached for failed; predictive processing now gives the idea a mechanism, a name and five tests.

item.title: Self-extinguishing maintenance: treatments that stop because they are working, and the relapse that follows
item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
item.description: Some problems only stay fixed while you keep treating them — a gap between two teeth, toes pressed too tight. The treatment works, the problem vanishes, it looks cured, you stop, and it comes back. This research named the cycle and the mistake behind it.

item.dc:creator: Chris Telford
